stamp: EXPLORATORY. The stance κ gate is not passed.

intro.goal: This project asks how people at Bay Area public meetings feel about housing density and transit. Each statement was scored from -2, strongly opposed, to +2, strongly supportive, toward the proposal being discussed, and a second pass then recorded whether that proposal would add or restrict housing or transit, so a score against a moratorium counts as a score for more housing. Proposals about housing but not about building it, such as rent rules, are left out of that reading rather than counted with the sign they carry. The officials who ran the meeting are compared with the members of the public who spoke.
intro.scope: 15,961 statements were scored, from 692 meetings of 33 Bay Area bodies: city councils, county boards and transit boards. The window is one year and 2,285 hours of video. A statement is one speaker turn of at least 5 words, in an episode that passed the quality gate. Each was scored three times and the median was kept.
intro.note: Exploratory analysis. Stance and tone were coded by a large language model and have not been validated against human coders.

spend.text: Total spend to date $152: GPU transcription $18, stance coding $68, topic classifier $60, proposal direction $6

stance.title: Stance: the role gap
stance.stamp: EXPLORATORY. The stance κ gate is not passed.
stance.lede: The dais is where the elected officials or board members sit and run the meeting. Hostility is scored from 0 to 4 for each statement. The scale counts speech aimed at people rather than strength of disagreement. A score of 2 or higher counts as hostile.
headline: 4.9 % of public statements were coded hostile, against 0.3 % of dais statements.
74 of 100 dais statements with a stance score were coded exactly neutral, against 22 of 100 public statements.

role_pred.title: Telling officials from the public, without reading the transcript
role_pred.text: A second model is given 35 coded measures of what each speaker said, and none of the transcript. Its task is to pick the member of the public out of one public and one dais speaker. It picks correctly 8 times out of 10, against 5 times out of 10 for chance. What separates the two is how strong an opinion a statement carries, not which side it is on.
role_pred.detail: The features are stance, hostility, the twelve frames, sub-topic and length, and two of them do nearly all the work: dropping absolute stance costs 0.14 of AUC and dropping length 0.04, with nothing else over 0.02. Signed stance on its own is at chance: 0.44 by cluster, against 0.50 for a coin. So the model is not learning who is a NIMBY, it is learning who holds a position at all. Two caveats. Calibration does not travel: the ranking holds between bodies but the probabilities do not, at a slope of 0.63 out of body, so this is a measurement of how separable the two roles are and not a classifier anyone should point at a new city. And the target here is the diarization-cue role. Fitted against the audited role the same model reaches 0.86, but that number is circular. The audit is itself built from what a speaker says about who they are, so the model is partly predicting its own input.
role_pred.holdout: leave-one-body-out (every meeting of a body held out together)
role_pred.audited_note: The audited role is itself derived from what the speaker says about who they are, so a content model predicting it is partly predicting its own input. These AUCs are not comparable to the cue-role ones.

model_free.note: Model-free contrast, 2,000 episode-cluster bootstrap reps, under the reported role (corrected 2026-10-18 after role audit). Shares are among turns with a numeric stance. Turns with no stance to code are 19.5 % of public turns and 47.1 % of dais turns. Every tail gap is larger than under the older cue-phrase role, on both outcomes and in every family.
model_free.cue_note: The same contrast under the old diarization-cue role, kept as a sensitivity. It reproduces what this panel published before 2026-10-18 exactly, so the difference is the role column and nothing else.

caveats.name: The κ ≥ 0.6 hand-coding gate is not passed
caveats.text: No human has coded any of these turns. The 0.98 replicate κ is the instrument agreeing with itself (noise floor ≈ 2 %); the one cross-instrument check on record is κ 0.63 against a second codebook, same side 88 % of the time. Nothing here is a confirmatory result.

caveats.name: There is no staff role
caveats.text: Roles are dais / public / unknown. Staff reports are counted as dais, which moves the dais toward neutral. 472 unknown-role turns are outside the frame, and the computed role instrument (35 classifier episodes) is a separate, wider facet rather than more data.

caveats.name: The reported role is an audit, not a gold label
caveats.text: Added 2026-10-18. The public/dais split here is role_audit (rule ra-1), which prefers the codebook's SELF_ID over the diarization-cue role. SELF_ID is model output and no human has checked it. 7,119 of 15,961 turns (45%) say nothing about who the speaker is and keep the cue role, so the audited public bucket is still contaminated at an unknown rate. The measured error is a lower bound on the informative subset only. And the audit is a re-partition in both directions, not a cleanup: it admits cue-dais clusters as well as removing cue-public ones, and the public base with a stance *rises* from 206 to 227 clusters. Differences from the _cue numbers are not 'contamination removed'.

nimby.title: YIMBY / NIMBY
nimby.stamp: EXPLORATORY. The stance κ gate is not passed.
nimby.lede: Each statement is scored from -2 to +2 for how far it supports more housing or transit, with the sign flipped on proposals that would restrict either. A speaker is YIMBY when their statements average +0.5 or higher, NIMBY at -0.5 or lower, and neutral between. A speaker here is one voice at one meeting.
nimby.corrected: corrected 2026-10-18 after role audit; frame grown 2026-10-19 (S2)
headline: Of 227 public speakers, 45.8 % were YIMBY, 40.5 % NIMBY and 13.7 % neutral.
In 1 of the 7 body-and-route groups measured, the likely range on YIMBY minus NIMBY excludes zero. In the other 6 it does not.

role_side.title: Who takes a side
role_side.headline: Public speakers took a side on 81.1 % of the statements that carried a stance, against 32.5 % of dais statements. Of the statements that took a side, 52.1 % of public ones opposed more housing or transit, against 38.2 % of dais ones.
role_side.model_line: A statement took a side when its corrected stance score was 0.5 or more away from neutral. The scale runs from -2 for opposing more housing or transit to +2 for supporting more of it. Staff speakers are excluded from this measure.

steps.name: Took a side at all
steps.text: 8.72× the odds of taking a side, for a public statement against a dais one (likely range 6.52 to 11.83).

steps.name: Which side, given a side
steps.text: 1.51× the odds of opposing more housing or transit rather than supporting it, for a public statement against a dais one (likely range 1.07 to 2.14).

role_side.restated: Quote 1.51× for “more opposed”. Step 1 measures whether a statement took a side at all, not which side.
role_side.why: Behind the two steps: 81.1 % of public turns take a side rather than scoring inside the neutral band, against 32.5 % of dais turns; of the turns that do take one, 52.1 % of public turns come out against more housing or transit against 38.2 % of dais ones. The two steps are separate fits on their own rows and do not multiply together. Almost all the dependence in this corpus is inside meetings rather than between bodies: on the second step the spread between stretches of meeting is 0.98 and between meetings 0.56 on the log-odds scale, while the spread between bodies is 0 once meeting is in the model. Which is why the model groups turns by meeting and not by city. Renter share does not move either step: its interval covers zero on both, and so does its interaction with role. Staff speakers are dropped from these rows altogether, because they read reports rather than take positions, and a council member chairing an item is doing something other than taking one too, which is most of what the first step is measuring.

table.what: Took a side at all, of every turn with a stance
Against more housing or transit rather than for it, of the turns that took a side

role_side.table_note: Odds ratios are for a public turn against a dais one, with renter share, its interaction with role and the locate route also in the model, and with a baseline per body, per meeting and per stretch of meeting. Each likely range is a 95 % interval taken from the likelihood rather than from a standard error, which is why it is not symmetric around the estimate.
role_side.limits: The unit here is a scored turn, not a person, and both the stance score and the public/dais label are model output that no human has checked. The role label comes from what a speaker says about who they are. The first step is largely a measure of speech act rather than opinion: chairing, moving and reading a report are all neutral by construction, and they are things only the dais does. The second step's interval is slightly wider than the data require, because the optimiser stops just short of the likelihood's peak and the interval was taken at a loosened tolerance. And the permutation test once quoted for this gap has been withdrawn; the evidence here is this model and nothing else.

caveats.name: How a speaker gets a label, and what the label is not
caveats.text: A speaker is YIMBY at a mean corrected stance of ≥ +0.5, NIMBY at ≤ −0.5, neutral between. Housing and transit proposals both count, since the corrected score reads as support for more of either. Each route gets its own table and figure and nothing is pooled, because routes that read the same body can disagree.

caveats.name: What the correction did, and whether San Leandro drives the result
caveats.text: A separate pass read each stretch of discussion three times and recorded whether its proposal would add or restrict housing or transit; the score was flipped on the restricting ones, and rent rules, open public comment and stretches the three reads disagreed on were left out. 408 of 1212 stretches survive that, 54 of them with the sign flipped. Dropping San Leandro, the body whose rent-stabilisation items the old reading inverted, moves the split from 45.8 / 40.5 / 13.7 to 46.2 / 41.2 / 12.7.

caveats.name: Most speaker labels rest on one scored statement
caveats.text: 80.6 % of labels rest on exactly one scored statement, and a speaker averages 1.24 of them. A speaker here is one voice inside one meeting, as separated by the diarizer: one person split in two counts twice, and two people merged count once.

renter.title: Renter share
renter.stamp: EXPLORATORY. The stance κ gate is not passed.
renter.lede: Renter share is the renter-occupied share of a body's occupied housing units, from the American Community Survey.
headline: Renter share showed no clear link to what gets said at meetings.

A staff member in a California county government suggested renter share as a main predictor, as a lead for future work. Each body's NIMBY share was regressed on renter share, with median household income and population density as covariates. No predictor showed a clear effect: every likely range is a 95 % interval, and all three include zero. Renter share also showed no clear link to YIMBY share or to meeting time on housing density and transit. With 18 bodies in the fit, a small real effect could still be missed.

covariates.census_names: Alameda County, California; Contra Costa County, California; San Francisco County, California

model_table.model: NIMBY share ~ renter + log income + log density

model.stamp: EXPLORATORY — stance κ gate not passed (plan/SHOWCASE.md 4a)

results.label: NIMBY share ~ renter + log income + log density

caveats.name: How little this could have detected: n is the finding
caveats.text: “No relationship” here means “no relationship this design could see”. Each correlation rests on 15 to 20 bodies with a median of 18 scored public turns each, which could only have detected an effect several times larger than any plausible one. The 90 % interval on the NIMBY slope runs from a large negative effect to a moderate positive one, and so does the interval on every other outcome tested. Read the null as a statement about the sample size, not about renter share. And a sharp result here would still be a statement about cities rather than about the people who show up to speak at their meetings: the covariate is a body's whole renter share, not anything known about a speaker.

caveats.name: The rate correlations should not be quoted at all yet
caveats.text: Both rate rows are computed on the as-published 7-body complete-coverage set. The coverage test has since been fixed and the complete set is 5 bodies, so on a rerun today those rows fall to n = 3 on the classifier route. The local_asr and agenda_index rate figures drop below the 3-body floor entirely and have been moved to output/renter_share/_stale_pre_coverage_fix/.

caveats.name: Transit boards are marked hollow, and a councils-only panel is drawn beside each figure
caveats.text: A transit board's topic time mostly measures what it exists to do, so every figure draws the boards with hollow markers and carries a councils-only panel wherever one can be drawn above the 3-body floor. Read the councils-only panel first.

rates.title: Topic time per meeting-hour
rates.stamp: Rates are a measurement, not a model estimate. Each likely range is a 95 % episode bootstrap.
headline: The two transit boards gave housing density and transit the most meeting time: BART 29.14 and VTA 27.00 minutes of each meeting-hour.
Napa County gave them 1.78 to 2.48 minutes, depending on which route read the meeting.
Only 3 bodies have every meeting read and a published video length, so only those 3 have a rate.

caveats.name: Most of these rates are floors
caveats.text: Only bart, napa, samtrans, sausalito, vta have had every meeting read. Fremont, Hayward, Petaluma, Richmond, San Leandro and Santa Clara are part-read, so their rates are floors. samtrans, sausalito publish no video length, so they get no rate at all.

caveats.name: Which route read a body moves its rate as much as the body does
caveats.text: Hayward measures 0.65 min/h on one route, 1.73 on another and 4.17 on a third. BART is at 29.1 min/h and VTA at 27.0, and Napa at 1.8 to 2.2 on all three of its routes. So route is a column in every table here and nothing is pooled.

caveats.name: Density does not outweigh transit everywhere
caveats.text: An earlier draft said it did. Hayward on the classifier route is 0.1 density against 0.4 transit, and Petaluma's Swagit route 7.2 against 8.2.
